title: The Urinary System
intro: The urinary system cleans the blood: the kidneys filter it, take back what the body needs and send waste, extra salts and water out as urine. This unit covers the parts of the system and the nephron, the three steps that make urine, how the kidney makes dilute or concentrated urine, how ADH, aldosterone and the renin-angiotensin system keep water and salt in balance, kidney stones, and how the system forms in the embryo.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the function and organization of the urinary system, including the inside of the kidney and the parts of a nephron.
Describe glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion, and say where each mainly happens.
Contrast how the kidney makes dilute urine and concentrated urine.
Explain how the kidneys and hormones (ADH and aldosterone) keep water and salt in balance, including the renin-angiotensin system.
Describe the embryonic origins of the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra.

img.alt: Food and drink intake plus water made by cellular respiration flow into the blood, and an equal output leaves as urine. Urine carries nitrogenous waste (urea, made in the liver from ammonia), extra solutes (Na+, Ca2+, K+, Cl- and H+) and water.

steps.title: Removing waste, solutes and water
bullets: The urinary system **removes waste, excess solutes and water** from the body.
By doing this it keeps the **composition and volume of the blood** steady.
**Nitrogenous wastes** come from protein metabolism. The liver turns **ammonia** into **urea**, which leaves in the **urine**.
Urine also carries **excess solutes** from the blood (Na+, Ca2+, K+, Cl- and H+) and water.

steps.title: Water in must equal water out
bullets: Water comes **in** from food and drink, and is **produced** as a by-product of cellular respiration.
To keep **homeostasis**, water **output** must equal intake plus production.

boxes.text: Every cell dumps waste and salts into the blood. If nothing removed them, blood composition would drift away from what cells need.
Think of the kidneys as the blood's cleaning and bookkeeping service: they throw out waste and keep the water account balanced.
Urea is made in the LIVER from ammonia, not in the kidney (slide 2). The kidney only excretes it. Water production counts too: cellular respiration makes water.

sections.title: The parts of the urinary system

img.alt: Front view of the body showing the two kidneys with the renal artery and renal vein, the aorta and inferior vena cava, a ureter running down from each kidney to the bladder, and the urethra leaving the bladder.

steps.title: From kidney to urethra
bullets: The main organs are the **kidneys**. Each has an outer **cortex**, an inner **medulla** and a **renal pelvis**, where urine collects.
The **ureters** carry urine from each renal pelvis to the **urinary bladder**.
The **urethra** carries urine out of the body.

steps.title: The bladder and urination
bullets: The **urinary bladder** stores urine for a while. Its wall has **three layers of smooth muscle** with an **epithelial lining** inside.
Urination is controlled by the **micturition reflex**, which involves the bladder and both the **internal** and **external urethral sphincters**.

boxes.text: Urine path: Kidney, Ureter, Bladder, Urethra. 'K-U-B-U': the ureter comes before the bladder, the urethra after it.
Ureter vs urethra: two ureters (kidney to bladder), one urethra (bladder to outside) (slide 3). The renal pelvis is inside the kidney, not a separate organ.

images.alt: Front view of the body showing the two kidneys with the renal artery and renal vein, the aorta and inferior vena cava, a ureter running down from each kidney to the bladder, and the urethra leaving the bladder.

img.alt: A kidney cut in half: the outer cortex, the inner medulla made of cone-shaped regions, the renal pelvis in the middle draining into the ureter, and the renal artery and renal vein entering at the side.

steps.title: Cortex, medulla and renal pelvis
bullets: Cut open, a kidney shows the **cortex** on the outside, the **medulla** inside it and the **renal pelvis** in the middle, which drains into the **ureter**.
The **renal artery** brings blood in and the **renal vein** takes it out.

img.alt: Close-up of a wedge of kidney showing many nephrons with their coiled parts in the cortex and long loops dipping into the medulla, all draining into a collecting duct.

steps.title: Millions of nephrons
bullets: Kidneys are filled with functional units called **nephrons**.
Each kidney has **millions of nephrons**, spanning from the **renal cortex** to the **medulla**.
Each nephron is a **hollow tubule** with its own **blood supply**.
Nephrons **remove, filter and return fluid** to the circulating blood.

boxes.text: A nephron is the smallest unit that can make urine, so the kidney's work is the sum of millions of them working side by side.
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, not the whole kidney or the collecting duct (slide 4). Nephrons span BOTH the cortex and the medulla.

images.alt: A kidney cut in half: the outer cortex, the inner medulla made of cone-shaped regions, the renal pelvis in the middle draining into the ureter, and the renal artery and renal vein entering at the side.
Close-up of a wedge of kidney showing many nephrons with their coiled parts in the cortex and long loops dipping into the medulla, all draining into a collecting duct.

img.alt: One nephron: the glomerular capsule holding the glomerulus with afferent and efferent arterioles, the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle with descending and ascending limbs reaching into the medulla, the distal tubule, and the collecting duct emptying into the renal pelvis.

steps.title: From capsule to collecting duct
bullets: The tubule starts with the **glomerular capsule**, which holds the **glomerulus**, a network of capillaries where **fluid filtration** happens.
The **proximal tubule** runs from the capsule toward the medulla.
The **loop of Henle** **descends** into the medulla and **ascends** back into the cortex.
The **distal tubule** joins a **collecting duct**. Each collecting duct is **shared by several nephrons** and empties into the **renal pelvis**.

boxes.text: Proximal = near the start (the capsule). Distal = far from the start. The loop of Henle sits between them like a hairpin.
The collecting duct is shared by many nephrons and is not part of a single nephron's own tubule (slide 5). Filtration happens at the glomerulus, not in the loop.

images.alt: One nephron: the glomerular capsule holding the glomerulus with afferent and efferent arterioles, the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle with descending and ascending limbs reaching into the medulla, the distal tubule, and the collecting duct emptying into the renal pelvis.

img.alt: Blood supply of nephrons. The renal artery and vein branch through the kidney. At each glomerulus an afferent arteriole enters and an efferent arteriole leaves; peritubular capillaries wrap the proximal and distal tubules, and in some nephrons the vasa recta runs down beside the loop of Henle.

steps.title: Arterioles and capillaries
bullets: A **renal artery** and **renal vein** connect each kidney to the circulation.
**Afferent arterioles** enter the glomerular capsule; **efferent arterioles** leave it.
**Peritubular capillaries** surround the proximal and distal tubules.
The **vasa recta** runs **parallel to the loop of Henle**.

boxes.text: Afferent = Arrives, efferent = Exits.

The efferent arteriole leaves the glomerulus as an ARTERIOLE, not a vein, and then branches into peritubular capillaries or the vasa recta (slide 6). The vasa recta goes with the loop of Henle, not the collecting duct.

images.alt: Blood supply of nephrons. The renal artery and vein branch through the kidney. At each glomerulus an afferent arteriole enters and an efferent arteriole leaves; peritubular capillaries wrap the proximal and distal tubules, and in some nephrons the vasa recta runs down beside the loop of Henle.

img.alt: Animation of filtrate moving through a nephron. 1 Filtration: fluid moves from the glomerulus into its capsule. 2 Reabsorption: arrows carry material from the proximal tubule back to the blood. 3 Secretion: arrows carry material from the blood into the distal tubule. The fluid then runs down the collecting duct as urine.

steps.title: Filtration, reabsorption and secretion
bullets: **Glomerular filtration**: a **protein-free** solution of fluid and solutes moves **from the glomerulus into the glomerular capsule**.
**Tubular reabsorption**: **most** of the filtered fluid and solutes **return to the blood** through the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta.
**Tubular secretion**: certain solutes move **from the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta into the tubule**.

img.alt: A nephron with its capillaries and three numbered boxes: 1 glomerular filtration of water, ions, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate and wastes into the capsule; 2 tubular reabsorption back into the peritubular capillaries, mainly in the proximal tubule; 3 tubular secretion of some drugs, wastes and ions, mainly into the distal tubule.

steps.title: What moves in each step
bullets: Filtered: **water, ions, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate** and wastes such as **urea and creatinine**.
Reabsorbed: **water, amino acids, glucose, most ions** (including bicarbonate) and **some urea**, mainly in the **proximal tubule**.
Secreted: **some drugs, wastes and ions** (mainly hydrogen, ammonium and potassium), mainly into the **distal tubule**.

boxes.text: Filtering everything small and then taking back what is useful lets the kidney get rid of waste it never had to recognize in advance.
Filtration: blood to tubule. Reabsorption: tubule back to blood. Secretion: blood to tubule again, but by a different route (through the tubule wall).
Filtrate is protein-free (slide 7). Reabsorption moves things INTO the blood; secretion moves things OUT of the blood into the tubule. Do not swap them.

images.alt: Animation of filtrate moving through a nephron. 1 Filtration: fluid moves from the glomerulus into its capsule. 2 Reabsorption: arrows carry material from the proximal tubule back to the blood. 3 Secretion: arrows carry material from the blood into the distal tubule. The fluid then runs down the collecting duct as urine.

A nephron with its capillaries and three numbered boxes: 1 glomerular filtration of water, ions, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate and wastes into the capsule; 2 tubular reabsorption back into the peritubular capillaries, mainly in the proximal tubule; 3 tubular secretion of some drugs, wastes and ions, mainly into the distal tubule.

img.alt: The capillary wall of the glomerulus acts as a sieve. Water, ions, glucose and waste such as urea pass from the blood into the glomerular capsule. Cells and large proteins are too big and stay in the blood. High pressure drives filtration because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole.

steps.title: A sieve
bullets: The cells of the glomerular capillaries act like a **sieve**: plasma fluid passes through into the glomerular space.
Glomerular capillaries are **more permeable to water and small solutes** than other capillaries, but **less permeable to large proteins and cells**.
So **glomerular filtrate** has the same concentration of fluid and solutes as plasma, but **no large proteins or cells**.

img.alt: The glomerular capsule wrapped around the ball of glomerular capillaries. Blood flows in by the afferent arteriole and out by the efferent arteriole; small arrows show filtrate moving into the glomerular space and on into the proximal tubule. An inset shows podocytes covering the capillaries.

steps.title: What drives it and what controls it
bullets: Filtration is driven by **high blood pressure** in the glomerulus, because the **efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole**.
The filtration rate is regulated by **controlling the diameter of the afferent arterioles** and by the overall control of **blood flow** in the body.

boxes.text: Blood can flow in through a wide afferent arteriole faster than it can leave through a narrow efferent one, so pressure builds up in the glomerulus and pushes fluid out.
Filtrate is like plasma MINUS large proteins and cells, at the same concentration of small solutes (slide 9). It is the efferent arteriole that is narrower.

images.alt: The capillary wall of the glomerulus acts as a sieve. Water, ions, glucose and waste such as urea pass from the blood into the glomerular capsule. Cells and large proteins are too big and stay in the blood. High pressure drives filtration because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole.

The glomerular capsule wrapped around the ball of glomerular capillaries. Blood flows in by the afferent arteriole and out by the efferent arteriole; small arrows show filtrate moving into the glomerular space and on into the proximal tubule. An inset shows podocytes covering the capillaries.

img.alt: Bar chart of how much of each filtered substance goes back to the blood: all of the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate; almost all of the water and Na+; about half of the urea; and none of the creatinine.

steps.title: What is taken back
bullets: Most reabsorption happens in the **proximal tubule**.
**All** the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate, and **almost all** the water and Na+, are reabsorbed.
About **half of the urea** is reabsorbed, but some wastes (for example **creatinine**) are not.
Less water is reabsorbed further along, but the **distal tubule and collecting duct** are critical for **regulating water excretion**.
Proximal tubule cells have a **brush border** of **microvilli** that makes reabsorption more efficient.

img.alt: A proximal tubule cell between the tubule lumen and a capillary. ATP pumps Na+ out of the cell; Na+ diffuses into the capillary and in from the lumen; Cl- and water follow; glucose and amino acids are co-transported in with Na+ and then move on into the blood.

steps.title: How Na+ pulls the rest along
bullets: 1. **Na+ is actively transported out** of a proximal tubule cell.
2. That Na+ then **diffuses into the capillary**.
3. Na+ can then **diffuse into the cell from the tubule lumen**.
4. **Cl- follows** the electrical gradient.
5. **Water follows** by diffusion as solutes concentrate.
6. Energy from Na+ diffusion powers **active co-transport of glucose and amino acids** into the cell.

boxes.text: Pumping Na+ out of the cell keeps Na+ low inside it, so Na+ keeps flowing in from the lumen, and chloride, water, glucose and amino acids ride along.
Na+ is the engine; Cl-, water, glucose and amino acids are the passengers.

Only ONE step (Na+ out of the cell) uses ATP directly (slide 12). Glucose is co-transported with Na+, not pumped by its own ATP. Creatinine is NOT reabsorbed; urea is about half reabsorbed (slide 11).

images.alt: Bar chart of how much of each filtered substance goes back to the blood: all of the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate; almost all of the water and Na+; about half of the urea; and none of the creatinine.

A proximal tubule cell between the tubule lumen and a capillary. ATP pumps Na+ out of the cell; Na+ diffuses into the capillary and in from the lumen; Cl- and water follow; glucose and amino acids are co-transported in with Na+ and then move on into the blood.

img.alt: Arrows run from the peritubular capillary down into the distal tubule carrying penicillin, pesticides, drugs, K+, H+ and ammonium, which leave in the urine. The kidneys do not judge whether a substance is good for us.

steps.title: Blood to tubule
bullets: Most tubular secretion happens in the **distal tubule**.
Substances move into the tubule by **active or passive transport**, depending on the substance.
It is critical for removing **toxic or foreign substances** and **drugs** from the blood: for example **penicillin, pesticides, drugs, K+, H+ and ammonium**.
The kidneys **do not decide whether a substance is good for us** (for example antibiotics and drugs).

boxes.text: Secretion is a second chance to clear something from the blood, including things that were not filtered.
Most secretion is in the DISTAL tubule; most reabsorption is in the PROXIMAL tubule (slides 11, 13). Antibiotics are secreted too, which is why the kidneys clear them.

images.alt: Arrows run from the peritubular capillary down into the distal tubule carrying penicillin, pesticides, drugs, K+, H+ and ammonium, which leave in the urine. The kidneys do not judge whether a substance is good for us.

img.alt: A nephron in the cortex and medulla. Water leaves the descending loop of Henle; NaCl leaves the ascending loop and the distal tubule; without ADH the collecting duct keeps its water, giving a large volume of dilute urine.

steps.title: Making dilute urine
bullets: The **descending loop of Henle** is **permeable to water**. Water leaves because the **medulla has a high solute concentration**.
The **first part of the ascending loop** is permeable to **salt but not water**: Na+ diffuses out.
The **later part of the ascending loop** lets neither water nor salt through, so Na+ is **actively transported out**.
The fluid left in the tubule has **little salt but a lot of water**. Without ADH, it passes through as a **large volume of dilute urine**.

img.alt: A collecting duct passing through the medulla with ADH present: water leaves the duct by passive diffusion at several points, giving a low volume of concentrated urine.

steps.title: Making concentrated urine with ADH
bullets: When we are **dehydrated** (for example sweating without drinking), **blood solute concentration rises**.
This stimulates **ADH** (antidiuretic hormone) release from the **hypothalamus and posterior pituitary**.
ADH makes the **collecting duct more permeable to water**.
Water is then **passively reabsorbed** as the duct passes through the **salty renal medulla**, giving a **small volume of concentrated urine**.

boxes.text: The medulla is kept salty. Whether water leaves the collecting duct into it depends on one switch: ADH.
Descending: Drops water. Ascending: Adds salt to the medulla (removes salt from the tubule).
The ascending loop is NOT permeable to water (slide 14). ADH acts on the collecting duct and increases water permeability; it does not pump water. No ADH = dilute urine.

images.alt: A nephron in the cortex and medulla. Water leaves the descending loop of Henle; NaCl leaves the ascending loop and the distal tubule; without ADH the collecting duct keeps its water, giving a large volume of dilute urine.
A collecting duct passing through the medulla with ADH present: water leaves the duct by passive diffusion at several points, giving a low volume of concentrated urine.

img.alt: Three stone sizes. Small stones a few millimetres across pass out in the urine. Slightly larger stones can block a ureter. Large stones must be removed by surgery or broken up with ultrasonic waves. Risk factors: chronic dehydration and high sodium intake.

steps.title: Renal calculi
bullets: **Minerals** in urine can crystallize in the **renal pelvis**, forming **kidney stones** (renal calculi).
Most stay **small** (a few millimetres) and pass out in the urine.
Slightly larger stones may **block a ureter**, stopping urine from reaching the bladder.
Large stones must be **removed surgically** or **broken up with ultrasonic waves** before they can pass.
Common risk factors: **chronic dehydration** and **high sodium intake**.

boxes.text: Less water and more salt means more concentrated urine, so minerals crystallize more easily.
Stones form in the RENAL PELVIS (slide 16), and it is a ureter they block. Most stones are small and pass on their own.

images.alt: Three stone sizes. Small stones a few millimetres across pass out in the urine. Slightly larger stones can block a ureter. Large stones must be removed by surgery or broken up with ultrasonic waves. Risk factors: chronic dehydration and high sodium intake.

img.alt: A loop: blood solute concentration rises above the set point, the hypothalamus triggers thirst and the posterior pituitary releases ADH, the kidneys raise collecting duct permeability to water, water intake rises and renal water loss falls, bringing the concentration back down.

steps.title: A negative feedback loop
bullets: Water balance is kept by a **negative feedback loop**.
When **blood solute concentration rises**, **ADH** is secreted, the collecting ducts become **more permeable to water**, and **more water is reabsorbed**.
When **blood solute concentration falls**, **ADH secretion drops**, the collecting ducts become **less permeable**, and **less water is reabsorbed**.

img.alt: Animation of a negative feedback loop: blood solute concentration rises, ADH is secreted, collecting ducts become more permeable to water, more water is reabsorbed, and the concentration falls so less ADH is released. Thirst also rises when solutes rise.

steps.title: Following the loop
bullets: Each change pushes the solute concentration **back toward the set point**, which is what makes the loop negative feedback.
Changes in blood solute concentration also control **thirst**.

boxes.text: Negative feedback means the response cancels the change: concentrated blood triggers water saving, which dilutes the blood again.
High solute concentration = MORE ADH = MORE water reabsorbed = LESS urine (slide 17). Thirst is part of the same loop.

images.alt: A loop: blood solute concentration rises above the set point, the hypothalamus triggers thirst and the posterior pituitary releases ADH, the kidneys raise collecting duct permeability to water, water intake rises and renal water loss falls, bringing the concentration back down.

Animation of a negative feedback loop: blood solute concentration rises, ADH is secreted, collecting ducts become more permeable to water, more water is reabsorbed, and the concentration falls so less ADH is released. Thirst also rises when solutes rise.

sections.title: Salt balance and the renin-angiotensin system

img.alt: The renin-angiotensin system acts on the adrenal cortex, which releases aldosterone; aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct so more Na+ is reabsorbed into the blood. Aldosterone release is mostly not set by blood Na+ concentration.

steps.title: Aldosterone
bullets: Salt excretion is regulated by **aldosterone**, a **steroid hormone** from the **adrenal cortex**.
Aldosterone makes **more Na+ reabsorbed** from the **distal tubule and collecting duct**.
Its release is controlled mostly by the **renin-angiotensin system**, not by blood Na+ concentration.
The renin-angiotensin system controls **blood pressure and volume** directly (**vasoconstriction**) and indirectly (**aldosterone**). It involves the **kidneys, liver and lungs**.

img.alt: Angiotensinogen is converted by renin into angiotensin I, and angiotensin I is converted by ACE into angiotensin II.

steps.title: Making angiotensin
bullets: **Renin** is an **enzyme** made and released by the **juxtaglomerular apparatus** of the kidneys.

**Angiotensinogen**, a protein from the **liver**, is changed step by step: **renin** makes **angiotensin I**, then **ACE** (angiotensin-converting enzyme, found in the **lungs**) makes **angiotensin II**.

img.alt: The glomerulus and its capsule with the afferent arteriole and distal tubule touching at the juxtaglomerular apparatus; a close-up shows the renin-secreting cells in the arteriole wall.

steps.title: Where renin comes from
bullets: The juxtaglomerular apparatus is where the **afferent arteriole** meets the **distal tubule**, next to the glomerulus.
**Renin-secreting cells** sit in the wall of the arteriole there.

img.alt: A loop: blood volume falls, the kidneys release renin, renin turns angiotensinogen from the liver into angiotensin I, ACE in the lungs makes angiotensin II, which causes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure, and makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone so the kidneys save salt; ADH saves water.

steps.title: The whole system
bullets: When **blood pressure falls** in the afferent arteriole at the juxtaglomerular apparatus, **renin is released**, which leads to angiotensin being made.
Angiotensin causes **vasoconstriction** (mainly in arterioles), which **raises blood pressure** back up.
Angiotensin also makes the **adrenal glands release aldosterone**, so the kidneys **retain salt**, and it triggers **ADH-induced water retention**.

boxes.text: Saving salt also saves water, because water follows salt. That is how the system raises blood volume as well as pressure.
Liver makes the raw material (angiotensinogen), kidney cuts it (renin), lungs finish it (ACE).

Renin is an ENZYME from the kidney, not a hormone from the adrenal gland (slide 19). Aldosterone saves Na+; it is mostly controlled by the renin-angiotensin system, not by blood Na+ (slide 18). ACE is in the lungs.

images.alt: The renin-angiotensin system acts on the adrenal cortex, which releases aldosterone; aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct so more Na+ is reabsorbed into the blood. Aldosterone release is mostly not set by blood Na+ concentration.
Angiotensinogen is converted by renin into angiotensin I, and angiotensin I is converted by ACE into angiotensin II.
The glomerulus and its capsule with the afferent arteriole and distal tubule touching at the juxtaglomerular apparatus; a close-up shows the renin-secreting cells in the arteriole wall.

A loop: blood volume falls, the kidneys release renin, renin turns angiotensinogen from the liver into angiotensin I, ACE in the lungs makes angiotensin II, which causes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure, and makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone so the kidneys save salt; ADH saves water.

img.alt: A tree of what the mesoderm becomes. The intermediate mesoderm gives the kidney and gonads; chordamesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and lateral plate mesoderm give the other tissues.

steps.title: Where the parts come from
bullets: The **kidneys and ureters** come from the **intermediate mesoderm**.
The **urinary bladder and urethra** come from the **cloaca**, which comes from **endoderm**.

img.alt: Two stages of an embryo's kidney. The pronephros at the front and the nephric duct grow back toward the cloaca; mesonephros tubules form behind it; at the rear a ureteric bud grows from the duct into the metanephrogenic mesenchyme.

steps.title: Three stages of kidney
bullets: Kidneys develop in **three stages**; the first two are **transient**.
A **pronephric duct** forms from the intermediate mesoderm and **migrates caudally** (toward the rear).
At the front, **pronephric tubules** form from mesenchyme and then **degenerate**.
Further back, **mesonephric tubules** form, and then **most regress**.
At the rear, **ureteric buds** are induced by, and grow into, the **metanephrogenic mesenchyme**.

img.alt: A cycle: the ureteric bud grows into metanephric mesenchyme and branches; mesenchyme cells gather into a cap and a renal aggregate, which turns into a vesicle, then a tube that becomes the nephron with Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, proximal and distal tubules joined to the collecting duct.

steps.title: Building nephrons
bullets: The ureteric buds **branch (ramify)** and make the mesenchyme around them **condense**.
The **renal aggregates** go through a **mesenchymal-epithelial transition** and become a **renal vesicle**.
The vesicle **elongates** and its cells specialize to form the **nephron tubule**, which **connects to the ureteric bud**.

img.alt: Two side views of an embryo's lower body. First the cloaca receives the hindgut and nephric duct; then the urorectal fold divides it into the rectum and the urogenital sinus, whose upper part becomes the urinary bladder joined by the ureter.

steps.title: Bladder and urethra
bullets: The **cloaca** is the shared waste chamber for the intestine and kidneys.
In mammals a **septum** divides it into the **rectum** and the **urogenital sinus**.
Part of the urogenital sinus becomes the **urinary bladder**, another part the **urethra**.
The first stalks of the ureteric buds join the bladder and become the **ureters**.

boxes.text: Upper tract (kidney, ureter) = intermediate MESODERM. Lower tract (bladder, urethra) = ENDODERM via the cloaca.

Ureters come from the ureteric BUD stalks (mesoderm), even though they join the endoderm-derived bladder (slides 21, 24). Pronephros and mesonephros are temporary; the kidney that stays grows where the ureteric bud meets the metanephrogenic mesenchyme (slide 22).

images.alt: A tree of what the mesoderm becomes. The intermediate mesoderm gives the kidney and gonads; chordamesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and lateral plate mesoderm give the other tissues.

Two stages of an embryo's kidney. The pronephros at the front and the nephric duct grow back toward the cloaca; mesonephros tubules form behind it; at the rear a ureteric bud grows from the duct into the metanephrogenic mesenchyme.

Certain solutes move from the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta into the tubule, by active or passive transport.

High blood pressure in the glomerulus, because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole.
By changing the diameter of the afferent arterioles and by overall control of blood flow.
All the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. Almost all the water and Na+ too.
About half of the urea is reabsorbed; creatinine is not.
Microvilli on proximal tubule cells that increase the efficiency of reabsorption.
Na+ is actively transported out of the proximal tubule cell (using ATP), then diffuses into the capillary.

cards.front: How are glucose and amino acids reabsorbed?
cards.back: By active co-transport with Na+, powered by the energy of Na+ diffusing into the cell.
Penicillin, pesticides, drugs, K+, H+ and ammonium.
Descending: permeable to water. First part of ascending: permeable to salt but not water. Later ascending: neither, so Na+ is pumped out.
Released from the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary when blood solute concentration rises; makes the collecting duct more permeable to water.

cards.front: Why does water leave the collecting duct with ADH?
cards.back: The renal medulla keeps a high solute concentration, so water is passively reabsorbed once the duct is permeable.
Renal calculi: mineral crystals that form in the renal pelvis. Risk factors: chronic dehydration and high sodium intake.
Steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex; makes the distal tubule and collecting duct reabsorb more Na+.
An enzyme made and released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus when blood pressure falls in the afferent arteriole.
Made from angiotensinogen (liver) by renin then ACE (lungs). Causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.
Kidneys and ureters: intermediate mesoderm. Bladder and urethra: the cloaca (endoderm).

quiz.q: What is the main job of the urinary system?
options: To make red blood cells for the circulation
To digest proteins into amino acids
To remove waste, excess solutes and water from the body
quiz.why: It removes waste, excess solutes and water, which keeps blood composition and volume steady. Urea is made by the liver, not the urinary system.

quiz.q: Where is urea made?
options: In the bladder, from urine salts
In the lungs, from carbon dioxide
quiz.why: Ammonia from protein metabolism is converted into urea in the liver. The kidneys then excrete it.

quiz.q: Which list gives the path of urine in the right order?
quiz.why: Urine collects in the renal pelvis, goes down a ureter to the bladder, and leaves through the urethra.

quiz.q: What makes up the wall of the urinary bladder?
options: One layer of skeletal muscle and a lining of cilia
Three layers of smooth muscle with an epithelial lining
Only a layer of epithelial cells
quiz.why: The bladder wall has three layers of smooth muscle with an interior lining of epithelial cells.

quiz.q: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
quiz.why: Nephrons are the functional units. Each is a hollow tubule with its own blood supply, and each kidney has millions.

quiz.q: Look at the kidney. Which label matches the inner layer of cone-shaped regions?
quiz.why: The medulla is the inner layer, made of cone-shaped regions. The cortex is the outer layer and the renal pelvis is the central space.

img.alt: A kidney cut in half: the outer cortex, the inner medulla made of cone-shaped regions, the renal pelvis in the middle draining into the ureter, and the renal artery and renal vein entering at the side.

quiz.q: In which order does filtrate pass through a nephron?
options: Glomerular capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct
Glomerular capsule, distal tubule, loop of Henle, proximal tubule, collecting duct
Collecting duct, distal tubule, loop of Henle, proximal tubule, capsule
Proximal tubule, glomerular capsule, loop of Henle, collecting duct, distal tubule
Glomerular capsule, loop of Henle, proximal tubule, collecting duct, distal tubule
quiz.why: It starts in the capsule, goes through the proximal tubule, down and up the loop of Henle, through the distal tubule and into a collecting duct.

quiz.q: Which statement about the collecting duct is correct?
options: It is where glomerular filtration happens.
It belongs to only one nephron.
It is shared by several nephrons and empties into the renal pelvis.
It carries blood out of the glomerulus.
It runs beside the loop of Henle as the vasa recta.
quiz.why: Each collecting duct is shared by multiple nephrons and empties into the renal pelvis.

quiz.q: Which vessels run parallel to the loop of Henle?
quiz.why: The vasa recta runs parallel to the loop of Henle. Peritubular capillaries surround the proximal and distal tubules.

quiz.q: Which vessel carries blood INTO the glomerulus?
quiz.why: Afferent arterioles enter the glomerular capsule; efferent arterioles leave it.

quiz.q: Which process moves fluid from the glomerulus into the glomerular capsule?
quiz.why: Glomerular filtration moves a protein-free solution from the glomerulus into the glomerular capsule.

quiz.q: What does tubular secretion do?
options: Returns most filtered fluid to the blood
Moves certain solutes from the blood into the tubule
Pushes plasma into the glomerular capsule
quiz.why: Secretion moves certain solutes from the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta into the nephron tubule.

quiz.q: Which description of glomerular filtrate is correct?
options: It has more glucose than plasma and many red blood cells.
It is pure water with no solutes.
It has large proteins but no ions.
It has the same solute concentration as plasma but no large proteins or cells.
It is the same as urine.
quiz.why: The glomerular capillaries let water and small solutes through but hold back large proteins and cells.

quiz.q: Why is blood pressure high in the glomerulus?
options: The afferent arteriole is narrower than the efferent arteriole.
The vasa recta pumps blood into it.
The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent arteriole.
The collecting duct pushes fluid back.
quiz.why: Blood enters through a wider afferent arteriole and leaves through a narrower efferent arteriole, so pressure builds and drives filtration.

quiz.q: How is the filtration rate regulated?
options: By changing the number of nephrons each day
By ADH acting on the glomerulus
By changing the diameter of the afferent arterioles and by overall blood flow
By aldosterone acting on the capsule
quiz.why: Filtration rate is controlled by the diameter of the afferent arterioles and the overall control of blood flow.

quiz.q: Where does most tubular reabsorption happen?
quiz.why: Most reabsorption happens in the proximal tubule, whose cells have a brush border of microvilli.

quiz.q: Which substance is NOT reabsorbed from the filtrate?
quiz.why: All the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate and almost all the Na+ are reabsorbed. Some wastes such as creatinine are not.

quiz.q: About how much of the filtered urea is reabsorbed?
options: Exactly the same amount as glucose
quiz.why: About half of the urea is reabsorbed, while creatinine is not.

quiz.q: In the proximal tubule cell, which step uses ATP directly?
options: Water diffusing in from the lumen
Na+ being actively transported out of the cell
quiz.why: Na+ is actively transported out of the cell using ATP. The other steps are diffusion or co-transport powered by the Na+ gradient.

img.alt: A proximal tubule cell between the tubule lumen and a capillary. ATP pumps Na+ out of the cell; Na+ diffuses into the capillary and in from the lumen; Cl- and water follow; glucose and amino acids are co-transported in with Na+ and then move on into the blood.

quiz.q: How do glucose and amino acids get into a proximal tubule cell?
options: By simple diffusion through the brush border
By active co-transport powered by Na+ diffusion
quiz.why: Energy from Na+ diffusing into the cell permits active co-transport of glucose and amino acids.

quiz.q: Where does most tubular secretion happen?
quiz.why: Most secretion happens in the distal tubule, by active or passive transport depending on the substance.

quiz.q: Which group lists substances removed from the blood by tubular secretion?
options: Red blood cells and large proteins
Penicillin, pesticides, K+, H+ and ammonium
quiz.why: Secretion removes toxic or foreign substances and drugs, including penicillin, pesticides, drugs, K+, H+ and ammonium.

quiz.q: Which part of the loop of Henle is permeable to water?
options: The first part of the ascending loop
The later part of the ascending loop
Only the bend of the loop
quiz.why: The descending loop is permeable to water, so water leaves into the salty medulla. The ascending loop is not permeable to water.

quiz.q: What happens in the later part of the ascending loop of Henle?
options: Urea is secreted into the tubule.
Na+ is actively transported out, because the wall lets neither water nor salt through.
quiz.why: This part is impermeable to both water and salt, so Na+ must be actively transported out. The fluid left has little salt but a lot of water.

quiz.q: A person sweats a lot and does not drink. What happens?
options: ADH rises and the collecting duct becomes more permeable to water.
Blood solute concentration falls and ADH falls.
ADH rises and the collecting duct becomes less permeable to water.
Aldosterone stops and urine becomes dilute.
quiz.why: Dehydration raises blood solute concentration, which stimulates ADH. ADH makes the collecting duct permeable to water, so water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated.

quiz.q: Where do kidney stones form?
quiz.why: Minerals in urine can crystallize in the renal pelvis to form kidney stones (renal calculi). Larger ones can block a ureter.

quiz.q: In the water balance loop, what happens when blood solute concentration falls?
options: ADH secretion rises and more water is reabsorbed.
Aldosterone falls and the bladder empties.
ADH secretion falls and less water is reabsorbed.
Renin is released from the liver.
quiz.why: Lower solute concentration reduces ADH, the collecting ducts become less permeable to water, and less water is reabsorbed. This is negative feedback.

img.alt: A loop: blood solute concentration rises above the set point, the hypothalamus triggers thirst and the posterior pituitary releases ADH, the kidneys raise collecting duct permeability to water, water intake rises and renal water loss falls, bringing the concentration back down.

quiz.q: Which statement about aldosterone is correct?
options: It is a peptide hormone from the posterior pituitary.
It makes the collecting duct permeable to water.
It is mostly controlled by blood Na+ concentration.
It is an enzyme made by the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
It is a steroid from the adrenal cortex that increases Na+ reabsorption.
quiz.why: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex. It increases Na+ reabsorption from the distal tubule and collecting duct and is mostly controlled by the renin-angiotensin system.

quiz.q: Which enzyme turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II, and where is it found?
quiz.why: Renin turns angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I; ACE, found in the lungs, turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II.

img.alt: Angiotensinogen is converted by renin into angiotensin I, and angiotensin I is converted by ACE into angiotensin II.

quiz.q: Which embryonic tissue gives rise to the kidneys and ureters?
quiz.why: The kidneys and ureters come from the intermediate mesoderm. The bladder and urethra come from the endoderm-derived cloaca.

order.title: Where urine goes
order.prompt: Put the stops in order, from where urine collects to where it leaves the body.
order.why: Urine collects in the renal pelvis, goes down the ureter to the bladder for storage, and leaves through the urethra.

order.title: Through a nephron
order.prompt: Put the parts in the order filtrate passes through them.
order.why: Filtrate enters the glomerular capsule, flows through the proximal tubule, down and up the loop of Henle, through the distal tubule, and into a shared collecting duct that empties into the renal pelvis.

order.title: The renin-angiotensin system
order.prompt: Put the events in order, starting with a fall in blood pressure.
order.why: Low pressure at the juxtaglomerular apparatus releases renin. Renin turns angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, ACE in the lungs makes angiotensin II, and angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, so the kidneys save salt.

layers.name: Blood pressure falls at the juxtaglomerular apparatus
ACE in the lungs makes angiotensin II
Aldosterone is released and the kidneys retain salt

order.title: Building a kidney
order.prompt: Put the stages of kidney development in order.
order.why: The pronephric duct and pronephric tubules come first and degenerate, then mesonephric tubules form and mostly regress. Ureteric buds then grow into the metanephrogenic mesenchyme, which condenses into renal aggregates, becomes a renal vesicle, and forms the nephron tubule.

layers.name: Ureteric buds grow into the metanephrogenic mesenchyme
Nephron tubule forms and joins the ureteric bud

sort.title: Which process?
sort.prompt: Sort each description into filtration, reabsorption or secretion.

items.text: Leaves out large proteins and cells
Returns most filtered water to blood
Moves K+ and H+ from blood into the tubule

sort.why: Filtration moves fluid from the glomerulus into the capsule; reabsorption returns material to the blood, mostly in the proximal tubule; secretion moves solutes from the blood into the tubule, mostly in the distal tubule.

sort.title: Dilute or concentrated urine?
sort.prompt: Sort each condition into dilute urine or concentrated urine.
sort.why: Without ADH the collecting duct keeps its water and urine is dilute. Dehydration raises ADH, which opens the duct to water, so water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated.

sort.title: Which embryonic origin?
sort.prompt: Sort each structure by where it comes from.
sort.why: The kidneys, ureters and their precursors come from the intermediate mesoderm. The bladder and urethra come from the urogenital sinus of the endoderm-derived cloaca.
